Concise Clinical Note

Consult Summary:
27-year-old man evaluated minutes after a wasp/bee sting to the right arm; mild localized cutaneous reaction without objective airway compromise—consistent with uncomplicated localized allergic reaction; advised antihistamine therapy and safety-netting for anaphylaxis.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Subjective “struggling to breathe,” slight lip tingling/swelling, and local rash after single insect sting on right arm a few minutes prior to call.  
• Course: Symptoms appeared immediately; no progression during video visit; anxiety present.  
• Associated symptoms: “Weird” tongue sensation; denies stridor, voice change, dysphagia, or generalized urticaria.  
• Pertinent negatives: No prior anaphylaxis; no EpiPen; no food, pet, or environmental allergies reported.  
• Past medical history: Eczema; occasional anxiety/panic episodes.  
• Allergies: Penicillin (reaction details not discussed).  
• Medications: None; no antihistamine taken yet.  
• Social: Lives alone with a cat; computer scientist; no smoking/alcohol history discussed. Preventive care not addressed.

Examination:
• General: Alert, speaking full sentences without distress.  
• Airway/respiratory (video): Normal breathing pattern; no audible stridor; lips and oral cavity appear normal; no visible tongue or oropharyngeal edema.  
• Skin: Right arm—puncture mark with mild erythematous, blotchy rash; no appreciable swelling, warmth, or spreading erythema.  
• Vitals: Not recorded.

Impression:
Primary diagnosis: Localized allergic reaction to insect sting—high likelihood given isolated cutaneous findings and absence of systemic compromise.  
Differential considerations:  
1. Early IgE-mediated anaphylaxis—medium likelihood; rapid onset and reported lip/tongue sensations warrant vigilance despite normal exam.  
2. Anxiety-related dyspnea—medium likelihood; subjective breathlessness without objective signs and known anxiety history.

Plan:
• Pharmacologic: Begin oral antihistamine—chlorphenamine 4 mg up to 6×/day or once-daily nonsedating alternative, OTC.  
• Education/Safety net: Reviewed red-flag symptoms (lip/tongue swelling, stridor, progressive breathing difficulty, spreading rash, heat/pain suggesting infection). Advised immediate A&E attendance if these occur or rapid deterioration is noted; otherwise contact GP.  
• Infection watch: If arm redness spreads/becomes hot, consider review for possible antibiotics.  
• Documentation: Provided patient information link on anaphylaxis.  
• Follow-up: No routine appointment scheduled; patient to re-contact service if symptoms progress or recurrent reactions develop.

Quality checks:

● Missing but expected elements: Objective vital signs; detailed penicillin reaction history; current medication list, smoking/alcohol status; exact follow-up timeframe.  
● Transcript–DDx conflicts: None noted—both sources align on localized reaction with need to monitor for anaphylaxis.  
● Transcript quality: Clear overall; minor repetitions and conversational noise; objective clinical data (vitals) limited by video format.
